standard.title: Developing Historical Inquiry Questions
standard.description: develop and modify a range of historical questions about the past to inform historical inquiry
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can develop and modify historical questions to inform inquiry at Year 9 level — scoping questions for a specific investigation and adjusting them based on source availability.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students develop a range of historical questions requiring historical argument, modify them in response to source suitability and scope, and evaluate whether questions are appropriately calibrated for the investigation.

nodes.label: Developing questions that require historical argument
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop a range of historical questions — a key question and related sub-questions — about an aspect of the past that require historical argument rather than factual retrieval.
nodes.minimum_width: Develop a key question and at least two related sub-questions for an inquiry topic; explain why each requires historical argument rather than simple factual recall.
nodes.typical_width: Develop a structured range of questions including a key question and related sub-questions for a chosen inquiry topic; identify, plan and begin investigating a specific historical question or issue; distinguish questions that require historical argument (cause, significance, change, perspective, interpretation) from those that require only factual recall.
wider: Develop inquiry questions for a topic with contested or incomplete sources — practising how to formulate researchable questions when the evidentiary record is uneven or politically sensitive

Compare the question structures used by professional historians for different purposes (academic monograph, public history exhibition, documentary), examining how purpose and audience shape what questions historians ask
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish argument-requiring questions from factual questions will develop research plans that cannot produce historical argument — the work of the entire inquiry collapses if the question doesn't require interpretation. This is the entry condition for meaningful historical inquiry.

response_modes.reason: Explicitly teach the distinction between questions that require argument ('Why did...', 'To what extent...', 'How significant was...') and those that require only retrieval ('When did...', 'Who was...'). Have students categorise example questions before attempting to write their own.

success_criteria: Develop a key question and at least two sub-questions for an inquiry topic
Explain why each question requires historical argument rather than factual recall
Identify the type of historical thinking each question demands (causation, significance, continuity/change, perspective, interpretation)

nodes.label: Modifying and scoping questions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can modify historical questions in response to source suitability and evaluate whether questions are appropriately scoped for the investigation.
nodes.minimum_width: Modify at least one question in response to source availability or scope constraints and explain the reason for the modification.
nodes.typical_width: Modify key questions and sub-questions in response to the suitability of available sources; determine whether questions are too broad or too narrow given the requirements of the investigation and the sources available; practise iterative question refinement — adjusting scope, focus, or framing in response to what sources can actually answer.
wider: Practise question modification across topics of different scale — from local history to national to global — examining how scale affects what questions are researchable and what sources exist

Develop and refine questions for a topic where key sources are missing or inaccessible (e.g. oral history topics, First Nations history before written records), examining how historians adapt their questions to work with the available evidence

response_modes.reason: Question modification requires iterative practice. Use think-aloud modelling of the refinement process — showing students how a question changes across multiple drafts as the historian tests it against available sources — before expecting students to do this independently.

success_criteria: Modify at least one historical question in response to source availability or scope constraints
Explain why the modification was necessary and what the revised question enables
Evaluate whether a given question is appropriately scoped for a specific investigation, providing a reasoned judgment
